title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
purpose: It compiles the rulings and narrations on visiting the sick, the dying state, remembrance of death, and the sharp line between permitted weeping and forbidden wailing/lamentation.

points.text: The 'dying state' (siyaq) is defined as the moment when death draws near and the passage from this world to the hereafter is imminent, per the book interpreting the pillars.
entities: book of the interpretation of the pillars

points.text: Asked whether people may relocate to flee epidemic and plague believing they will escape it, Idris ibn Hasan answered that they may go wherever they wish, since the matter is in Allah's hand.

Jafar ibn Sulayman's epistle 'The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations' — written to admonish his heedless followers among the people of the island of Yemen where he had settled — rebukes them for being slow to visit the sick, citing the pillars' report from the Commander of the Faithful that seventy thousand angels pray for a Muslim who visits a sick person from the hour of his visit until sunset (or sunrise, if by night).
entities: The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations

points.text: The Prophet forbade the visitor from eating in the sick person's presence, and Allah nullifies (in another wording, casts behind him) the reward of such a visit, the stated reason being that eating in a poor sick man's house burdens him and inwardly galls his household.
Whoever knows such rulings is obliged to pass them on, since the learned are few, and the one who gives the warning has thereby discharged his duty.

From 'Ali's four hundred points of conduct: one must not sleep in the prohibited posture nor on one's face (and the sleeper on his face is to be woken), a woman is not to sleep stretched on her back, and refuge is sought from severe affliction because the gravest affliction is loss of one's religion.

On lifespans: they are fixed terms that neither increase nor decrease, yet the reported 'increase and decrease' is sound in the sense that what is diminished in the past cycle is added in the future one.

The saying that 'the wretched is he whom the Hour overtakes while alive and not yet dead' is interpreted to mean that the Hour comes upon him while he is still in the animal (bahimi) condition, not having passed to the angelic life.

Husayn ibn Idris ruled, answering Hasan ibn Nuh's tenth question, that a living formed child in a dead mother's womb must be extracted if a skilled woman is present and it is possible, or if the fetus is six months or more with hope of life; otherwise the mother is not buried until the child's death is confirmed.

'Ali taught frequent remembrance of death, the rising from graves and the standing before Allah so that calamities sit lightly, described fever as death's forerunner and Allah's prison on earth which strips away sins as hair is stripped from a camel's pores, and said that a Shi'a who departs from a prohibition is afflicted in property, child or self so that his sins are purged before meeting Allah — the dead of their Shi'a being a truthful witness (siddiq shahid).

Innovations of mourning are condemned: no shaving hair, lighting lamps or cutting nails for the dead; placing weapons beside the corpse or holding a vigil beside it obligatory has 'no reliance to be placed upon it'; and the gathering of women to lament for nights and days with singing and play, as if it were a prescription at fixed times, disgraces the believers before Allah and His friends.

Wailing is forbidden by narration: Jafar ibn Muhammad bequeathed that no cheek be struck and no collar torn for him (the woman who tears her collar has a rent in Hell that grows as she adds to it), 'Ali wrote to Rifaah ibn Shaddad his judge over al-Ahwaz to forbid wailing where he held authority, and the Prophet named two accursed voices — howling at calamity and a voice raised at a blessing — i.e. wailing and singing.

The account of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah shows the dead/dying are punished by the living's words: he saw an angel with a fiery iron mace who struck at his skull each time a woman shrieked 'O my mountain!' or 'O my might!', desisting only when he answered 'No, rather Allah', and the Prophet confirmed it saying, 'What is the matter with your dead, that they suffer by the words of your living?'

The decisive distinction: the Prophet wept at the death of his child and declared he had not forbidden weeping but only wailing and lamentation, weeping being a tenderness and mercy Allah places in whom He wills; he licensed tears at calamity ('the soul is stricken, the eye sheds tears') while commanding only speech pleasing to Allah and forbidding foul speech (hujr).

Correspondingly, the singing forbidden at calamity is permitted at weddings and banquets solely to distinguish lawful marriage from fornication — the Prophet, hearing music among the Banu Zurayq, approved it, saying there is no secret marriage until smoke is seen or a tambourine heard, and that the beating of the tambourine is what separates nikah from sifah.

'Ali commanded households to speak well over their dead, citing Fatimah — when the daughters of Hashim mourned with her at her father's death she said 'Grieve with restraint, and hold fast to supplication' — and he ruled that whoever strikes his thigh at a calamity forfeits his reward.
